summary: This RFC describes the Certificate Management Protocol (CMP) for creating and managing X.509v3 certificates. It defines messages between clients and PKI components such as a Registration Authority and Certification Authority. It obsoletes RFC 4210 and RFC 9480.

plainLanguage.summary: CMP is the protocol a certificate authority and its clients use to talk about certificates: to ask for one, to get one, to replace a key that is about to expire, or to withdraw one. This document is the current version of that protocol. It replaces two earlier ones, keeps working with the previous version where it can, and adds support for a new kind of public key, the kind used to share a secret rather than to sign.

subtitle: How a client system asks a certificate authority for certificates, and how the authority checks the request.

tldr.problem: A public key infrastructure needs a protocol for the conversations that surround certificates: asking for one, receiving one, replacing a key that is about to expire, withdrawing a certificate, and handing over a new trust anchor.
tldr.mechanism: CMP defines those messages, each with a header, a body, optional protection and optional extra certificates. The core of the protocol is the initial registration exchange, in which a client proves it holds the private key for the public key it wants certified, and the authority issues the certificate and confirms the result.
tldr.outcome: The document obsoletes RFC 4210 and RFC 9480, adds support for certificates holding a key encapsulation mechanism public key, and uses the CMS EnvelopedData structure instead of the older EncryptedValue. It keeps compatibility with CMP version 2 and introduces version 3 for the syntax changes.

today: RFC 9810 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2025. It obsoletes RFC 4210 and RFC 9480, and it updates RFC 5912. Compatibility with CMP version 2 is kept wherever possible, and version 3 was introduced for the changes to the ASN.1 syntax. The algorithms and message profiles for the protocol are specified separately, in RFC 9481 and in the appendices of this document.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 9810 specifies the Certificate Management Protocol (CMP) for the Internet X.509 public key infrastructure. It defines protocol messages for certificate creation and management, and the interactions between client systems and PKI components such as a Registration Authority (RA) and a Certification Authority (CA). The document is the third in the line: it lists the ways in which RFC 4210 differed from RFC 2510, it includes the updates made by RFC 9480, and it obsoletes both RFC 4210 and RFC 9480.

The headline changes are support for certificates that contain a key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) public key, and the use of the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) type EnvelopedData instead of the older EncryptedValue, which gives the protocol better agility in its algorithms. Backward compatibility with CMP version 2 is kept wherever possible, and CMP version 3 is introduced for the changes to the ASN.1 syntax: support for EnvelopedData, certification confirmation with a hash algorithm, POPOPrivKey with agreeMAC, and RootCaKeyUpdateContent in key update announcement messages.

The document also adds a Key Generation Authority as an entity of its own, extends the discussion of Certificate Transparency logs, and introduces RootCaKeyUpdateContent as an alternative to using a repository to acquire a new root CA certificate, deprecating the older CAKeyUpdAnnContent for that purpose. It adds a new CMP information type for the KEM ciphertext used to protect messages, and adds subsections on the necessity of proof of possession, on perfect forward secrecy, on the recurring use of KEM keys for message protection, and on the use of CT logs.
sections.plainLanguage: CMP is how a certificate authority and its clients talk about certificates: to ask for one, to get one, to replace a key that is about to expire, or to withdraw one. This document is the current version of that protocol. It replaces two earlier ones, keeps working with the previous version where it can, and adds support for a new kind of public key, the kind used to share a secret rather than to sign.

sections.title: The PKI Management Model
sections.content:
The document defines the parties that take part in PKI management before it defines any messages. The end entity is the entity a certificate is issued to, typically named in the subject or subjectAltName field. End entities are not only people: they include applications, such as those that use IKE or IPsec, and devices, such as routers and industrial control systems. That matters for the protocol, because application software is far more likely to know exactly which certificate extensions it needs than a person is.

The CA is the entity that issues the certificate, and it often belongs to the same organisation as the end entities it supports. A root CA is a CA that is directly trusted by an end entity, so that acquiring its public key takes an out-of-band step; the term does not imply that it sits at the top of any hierarchy. A subordinate CA is a CA that is not the root CA for the end entity in question.

A Registration Authority (RA) may also be involved. Its functions vary, and may include identity checking, token distribution, checking certificate requests and authenticating their origin, revocation reporting, name assignment and archival of key pairs. The document treats the RA as an OPTIONAL component: when there is none, the CA is assumed to do the RA's work, so the protocol looks the same from the end entity's point of view. A Key Generation Authority (KGA) is an optional entity that generates key pairs on behalf of end entities and therefore knows both the public and the private part; without one, the CA does that job.

Each end entity needs secure local access to at least its own name and private key, the name of a CA that it trusts directly, and that CA's public key or a fingerprint of it. The document calls that local trusted storage the end entity's TEE, also known as a Personal Security Environment, and a certification response message may be used to fill it.
sections.plainLanguage: Four kinds of party appear: the end entity that wants a certificate, the CA that issues it, an optional Registration Authority that checks the request first, and an optional Key Generation Authority that makes the key pair for the end entity. The end entity also needs somewhere safe to keep its own key and the public key of the CA it trusts.

sections.title: Requirements on PKI Management
sections.content:
The protocols meet nine requirements on PKI management, and those requirements set the shape of the whole specification.

  • Management must conform to the ISO/IEC 9594-8 standards.
  • It must be possible to update any key pair regularly without affecting any other key pair.
  • The use of confidentiality must be kept to a minimum, to ease acceptance in environments where strong confidentiality would cause regulatory problems.
  • Different industry-standard cryptographic algorithms must be usable, so that any given CA, RA or end entity may in principle use whichever algorithms suit its own key pairs.
  • The protocols must not preclude the generation of key pairs by the end entity, by a KGA or by a CA.
  • They must support the publication of certificates by the end entity, by an RA or by a CA.
  • They must support the production of Certificate Revocation Lists, by letting certified end entities request revocation in a way that does not make denial-of-service attacks simpler.
  • They must be usable over a variety of transports, specifically including email, HTTP, MQTT, CoAP and offline or non-networked file transfer.
  • Final authority for certification creation rests with the CA: no RA or end entity can assume that a certificate it receives contains what it asked for, because a CA may alter field values or add, delete or alter extensions according to its policy.

That last requirement has a consequence the document spells out: every PKI entity must be able to handle a response in which the certificate issued differs from the one requested, for example because the CA shortened the validity period. And where policy requires it, the certificate must not be published until the requesting entity has reviewed and accepted it or the proof of possession is complete.
sections.plainLanguage: These nine rules shape everything else. A key pair must be replaceable without disturbing the others, each party may use whichever algorithms it likes, key pairs may be made anywhere, revocation must be possible without making denial of service easy, the protocol must run over email, HTTP, MQTT, CoAP or a file copy, and the authority always has the last word on what a certificate says.

sections.title: Initial Registration and Certification
sections.content:
No single scheme suits every first certificate, because a CA may have many policies and the end entity may be a person, a router or an application. The document classifies the schemes by three criteria: where the exchange starts, whether the messages from the end entity are authenticated, and where the key pair is generated. A fourth criterion follows from the flow: whether the end entity confirms that it received the certificate.

Two schemes are described. In the centralized scheme, initiation occurs at the certifying CA, no online authentication is required, the key pair is generated at the CA, and no confirmation is needed. The only message required is one from the CA to the end entity, and it must contain the entire TEE for that end entity. Some out-of-band means must exist so that the end entity can authenticate the message and decrypt any encrypted values in it.

In the basic authenticated scheme, initiation occurs at the end entity, message authentication is required, the key pair is generated at the end entity, and a confirmation is recommended. The end entity is given an Initial Authentication Key and a reference value out of band, generates its key pair, creates a certification request, protects the request with that key and sends it. The CA or RA verifies and processes the request, creates a response and returns it. The end entity then creates a confirmation and sends it, and the CA or RA answers with an optional acknowledgement. The Initial Authentication Key may be a symmetric key or an asymmetric private key with a certificate issued by another PKI that is trusted for this purpose; establishing that trust is out of scope. Where verification of the confirmation message fails, the CA or RA MUST revoke the newly issued certificate if it has been published or otherwise made available.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two basic ways to get a first certificate. In the simple one, the authority generates the key and sends everything to the device in a single message that the device authenticates some other way. In the more common one, the device generates its own key, protects its request with a secret key it was given in advance, and confirms at the end that it received the certificate. If that confirmation does not check out, the authority must withdraw the certificate.

sections.title: Proof of Possession
sections.content:
Proof of Possession (POP) is where the CA or RA checks that the end entity really holds the private key matching the public key in the requested certificate. The document is blunt about the need for it: because many operational protocols, the electronic mail protocols being an example, do not check the binding between an end entity and its private key, that binding can only be assumed to have been verified by the CA or RA. If it is not verified, the certificates in the Internet PKI end up being somewhat less meaningful. A CA or RA is free to choose how it enforces POP, with out-of-band procedures or with in-band messages, but it is REQUIRED that it enforce POP by some means.

The method depends on the type of key. For a signature key, the end entity signs a value. For an encryption key, the end entity can hand over the private key, for example for archiving, or can be challenged to decrypt a value. The challenge is direct when the CA or RA issues a random challenge and requires an immediate response, and indirect when the CA issues a certificate that is encrypted for the end entity, and the end entity shows it can decrypt that certificate in the confirmation message. The document encourages the indirect method, because it requires no extra messages: the proof fits into the request, response and confirmation triple. For a key agreement key, the end entity and the CA or RA establish a shared secret key together. For a KEM key, the end entity can hand over the private key or can show that it can decapsulate a ciphertext, derive the shared secret key from it, decrypt the certificate encrypted with that key and send a hash of the certificate in the confirmation message.

An end entity may also send the proof to an RA, which then tells the CA that the proof has been received and validated, although some policies allow only the CA to verify POP.
sections.plainLanguage: Proof of possession is the check that the person or device asking for a certificate really holds the matching private key. For a signing key, that means signing something. For an encryption key, it means decrypting something the authority sent. For a key agreement or key encapsulation key, it means working out a shared secret with the authority. The document prefers the method that needs no extra messages: the authority sends a certificate that only the right holder can decrypt, and the holder proves it in the last message of the exchange.

sections.title: The PKI Message
sections.content:
Every message used for PKI management has the same structure: a header, a body, optional protection and optional extra certificates. The header holds what is common to many messages: the protocol version, the sender, the recipient, and optionally the message time, the protection algorithm, identifiers for the sender's and the recipient's keys, a transaction identifier, a nonce from each side, free text and general information. If a message is protected, the header information is protected as well, because the protocol makes no assumption that the transport is secure.

Some details matter in practice. If the sending entity does not yet know its own name, as in the first request from an end entity, the sender field holds a NULL-DN and the senderKID field holds a reference number that tells the receiver which shared secret to use. The transaction identifier ties the messages of one exchange together; a client is RECOMMENDED to fill it with 128 bits of (pseudo-)random data at the start of a transaction, and a server that finds the identifier already in use must answer with an error carrying the failure information transactionIdInUse.

The body holds the information specific to the message. The protection field holds the bits that protect the message, and may carry a signature, a MAC, a Diffie-Hellman key pair or a key encapsulation. The extraCerts field holds certificates that may be useful to the recipient, for instance the certificates an end entity needs to verify its own new certificate when the CA that issued it is not a root CA for that end entity. That field does not necessarily contain a certification path, so the recipient may have to sort and select from the certificates it is given.
sections.plainLanguage: Every CMP message has three or four parts: a header that says who is talking to whom and which version of the protocol is in use, a body that says what the message is about, optional protection that makes the message tamper-evident, and optional extra certificates that the sender thinks the receiver will need.

sections.title: Mandatory PKI Management Functions
sections.content:
Section 6 lists the functions that every end entity and CA or RA implementation must be able to provide, although they need not be carried out with the messages of Section 5 when another means suits the environment.

A newly created root CA at the top of a hierarchy produces a self-certificate, and, so that end entities that do not receive it out of band can still check it, a fingerprint of that certificate, which an end entity can then use to verify the certificate and the other attributes in it. CA keys have a finite lifetime and must be updated periodically, and the certificates NewWithNew, NewWithOld and OldWithNew can be issued to help end entities move from the old root CA certificate to the new one and the other way round. Initialising a subordinate CA works like initialising an end entity, with the addition that the subordinate CA must also produce an initial revocation list. Before issuing any certificates, a newly established CA must produce empty versions of each revocation list it will produce, to be published periodically.

Any PKI entity may ask a CA for information about its current status, and the CA must answer with at least everything that was asked for, or convey an error. Over PKI messages the request is a GenMsg, the response a GenRep and the error an Error message, protected with a MAC based on shared secret information or with a signature. Cross-certification lets two CAs issue a certificate for each other. It is essentially a one-way operation: the responder CA generates an authorisation code and passes it to the requester CA out of band, the requester uses it to start the exchange with a cross-certification request protected by a MAC derived from the code, the responder answers with a cross-certification response carrying a new certificate for the requester signed with its own key, the requester confirms with a certConf message, and the responder acknowledges with a pkiconf message.

An end entity needs at least two steps to initialise itself: acquiring information about the PKI, which means the current root CA public key and, if the certifying CA is not that root CA, the certification path with the relevant revocation lists, and verifying one root CA public key out of band. After that it may request a certificate with a certification request, usually protected with its own digital signature, and the CA returns the certificate in a CertRepMessage. When a key pair is about to expire, the end entity may ask for a key update with a key update request, and the CA returns the new certificate in a key update response, which is syntactically identical to a CertRepMessage.
sections.plainLanguage: Every implementation has to support a list of operations. A root CA publishes a self-certificate and a fingerprint of it so that clients can check it. A CA whose key is about to expire issues certificates that let clients move from the old key to the new one. A CA publishes empty revocation lists before it issues any certificates. Two CAs can issue certificates for each other, using an authorisation code that one passes to the other outside the protocol. And once a client is set up, it can ask for a new certificate, ask for a replacement key, or ask for a certificate to be withdrawn.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations run to eleven subsections, and the recurring theme is that private keys and shared secrets have to be handled carefully.

On proof of possession, the document explains that a CA must check that the name and the public key belong to the end entity, because an entity holding a private key that obtains a certificate containing the corresponding public key issued for a different entity can authenticate as the entity named in the certificate, which facilitates masquerading. It also warns that an end entity asked to prove possession of a decryption key is effectively challenged to decrypt something, and that implementations should be very careful about decrypting arbitrary ciphertext and revealing the recovered plaintext, because such a practice can lead to serious security vulnerabilities. The client MUST return the decrypted values only if they match the expected content type. Exposing a private key to the CA as a POP technique carries its own risks, so it should be used only when archival is wanted and, where appropriate, the user should be told that the CA will hold a copy.

On key exchange, the document describes a small subgroup attack in which a malicious end entity chooses Diffie-Hellman parameters that let it derive part of the CA's private key during a key archival or key recovery operation. The simple remedy, which is RECOMMENDED, is for the CA to generate a fresh Diffie-Hellman key pair for each end entity it interacts with. On long-term secrecy, encrypted private keys and revocation passphrases are transferred with CMS EnvelopedData, which does not offer perfect forward secrecy, so where long-term security is needed the messages SHOULD travel over a mechanism that does, such as TLS with appropriate cipher suites. A CA should not reuse its certificate signing key for other purposes, and nonces, private keys and shared secrets must come from a cryptographically secure random source.

The last subsections cover trust anchors, extended key usages and Certificate Transparency. A provider of trust anchors MUST NOT include a certificate to be trusted in a CMP message unless the deployment can ensure the receiving end entity loads it into its trust store; the end entity MUST authenticate the message sender with existing trust anchors, without needing new trust anchor information from the message itself, and MUST verify that the sender is an authorized source of trust anchors. A CA that supports indirect POP MUST NOT publish final certificates to CT logs before it has received the confirmation that completes the proof, because a malicious actor could fetch the certificate from the log and use it to spoof that confirmation. Precertificates may be published, and a certificate published to a log must be revoked if the required confirmation cannot be verified.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of this section is about keys and secrets. The authority must be sure that the applicant holds the private key, and it must not decrypt arbitrary data for an applicant without checking what the result is, because that habit has caused real vulnerabilities. The authority should use a fresh Diffie-Hellman key pair for each client, keep its signing key for signing only, and use a genuinely random source for keys and nonces. The last part is about trust anchors: a certificate sent in a message is not a trust anchor until the receiver has loaded it into its trust store, and a certificate published to a transparency log before the proof of possession is finished must be withdrawn if that proof never arrives.

viz.caption: THE ENTITIES IN A PKI MANAGEMENT SYSTEM

items.title: End entity
items.text: The party a certificate is issued to: a person, an application or a device.

items.title: CA
items.text: The party that issues the certificate. It has the last word on its contents.

items.title: Root CA
items.text: A CA that an end entity trusts directly, so its public key has to arrive out of band.

items.title: Subordinate CA
items.text: A CA that is not the root CA for the end entity in question.

items.title: Registration Authority
items.text: An optional component that checks requests, reports revocations and assigns names.

items.title: Key Generation Authority
items.text: An optional component that generates key pairs on behalf of end entities.

messages.label: IAK
messages.note: The Initial Authentication Key and a reference value are delivered out of band.

messages.label: CR
messages.note: The certification request, protected with the Initial Authentication Key.

messages.label: CP
messages.note: The certification response, carrying the new certificate.

messages.label: CERT CONF
messages.note: The end entity confirms that it received and accepted the certificate.

messages.label: CONF ACK
messages.note: The optional acknowledgement of that confirmation.

viz.caption: HOW POSSESSION IS PROVED FOR EACH KEY TYPE

columns: How the end entity proves it holds the private key

cells: It signs a value with the private key.
It decrypts a challenge, or proves it can decrypt a certificate encrypted for it.
It and the authority establish a shared secret key together.
It decapsulates a ciphertext, derives the shared secret key and decrypts the certificate.

viz.caption: THE PKI MESSAGE STRUCTURE, VERBATIM FROM SECTION 5.1

data.title: PKIMessage
data.code:
PKIMessage ::= SEQUENCE {
   header           PKIHeader,
   body             PKIBody,
   protection   [0] PKIProtection OPTIONAL,
   extraCerts   [1] SEQUENCE SIZE (1..MAX) OF CMPCertificate
                     OPTIONAL
}
